guideTitle: 6 Best Bird Feeder Poles With Squirrel Baffles in 2026
metaTitle: 6 Best Bird Feeder Poles With Baffles (2026)
metaDescription: Six bird feeder poles with squirrel baffles compared on height, prong base, hook count and load limits to hang feeders safely out of squirrel reach.
introParagraphs: A pole with a baffle is the most dependable way to protect a bird feeder from squirrels, because it stops them before they reach the feeder at all. Wildlife guidance generally suggests mounting the feeder about 5 feet off the ground with a wide cone baffle below it, at least 10 feet from trees or structures squirrels can jump from. The pole itself has to be stable enough to hold up in wind and under load.

This lineup covers six poles. The eWonLife stands 92 inches with a 16.5 inch spring baffle, a nine-prong base and four hooks, two FEED GARDEN models bring 19 inch baffles with double or triple hooks, two Gtongoko models publish load limits by height, and the Phikrou is a 76 inch kit in 1 inch galvanized steel. Heights run from 76 to 92 inches when fully extended.

We evaluated each one based on product specs and buyer feedback, concentrating on base stability, baffle size, hook count and the load limits that decide what you can hang. Poles do not include feeders, so budget for the feeder you plan to hang and check its weight when full of seed before you pick a pole.

products.name: eWonLife 92 Inch Pole With Spring Baffle 9-Prong Base
products.description:
The eWonLife is a six-section pole that adjusts from 47 to 92 inches on a 1 inch diameter tube, topped by a 16.5 inch baffle with a built-in spring. The listing says the baffle sinks and wobbles to shake squirrels off, and its textured powder coat resists chewing and weather. The base uses nine reinforced steel prongs, compared with the five to seven on standard bases.

Four free-sliding shepherd hooks and a wide top platform let you hang several feeders or mount a birdhouse or camera feeder. It also includes a detachable bird bath and a mesh food tray, so you can set up a full station from one box. The tradeoff is that the 16.5 inch baffle is narrower than the 19 inch baffles on the FEED GARDEN and Gtongoko poles.

Nine prongs take more effort to push into hard ground, but they grip soil firmly in heavy rain or strong wind. Clean the bath and tray on a regular schedule and rinse the mesh weekly. Compared with the Phikrou at 76 inches it reaches 16 inches higher, and next to the FEED GARDEN triple hook it has four hooks against three.
products.bestFor: Windy or soft-soil yards that want a full feeding station.
cons: 16.5 inch baffle is narrower than 19 inch models

products.name: FEED GARDEN 92 Inch Double Hook Pole 19 Inch Baffle
products.description:
This FEED GARDEN pole combines a 19 inch cone baffle with a 5-prong base and double hooks. The baffle has a smooth surface to block squirrels, and the pole is premium alloy steel with a rust-resistant coating. The listing says it adjusts from 44 to 92 inches and that the five-prong base grips better than ordinary two-prong poles.

A 19 inch baffle is 2.5 inches wider than the eWonLife's 16.5 inch spring baffle, which makes it harder for a squirrel to bypass. Two hooks let you hang a feeder and a bath or planter. The tradeoff is fewer prongs than the eWonLife's nine, so firm soil matters more.

Assembly is tool-free in minutes by adding or removing pole sections. Slide the baffle on at 4 to 5 feet above the ground and wipe it down so it stays slick. Compared with the triple-hook FEED GARDEN it has one fewer hook, and next to the Gtongoko 5-prong it shares the 19 inch baffle but gives no per-hook load limit.
products.bestFor: Average yards that want a wide baffle and two hooks.
cons: Fewer prongs than the nine-prong eWonLife

products.name: FEED GARDEN 92 Inch Triple Hook Pole 19 Inch Baffle
products.description:
This FEED GARDEN adjusts from 44 to 92 inches and carries three hooks, so you can build a complete station with feeders, plants and decorations. The 19 inch cone baffle has a smooth surface, and the 5-prong base is described as stable in all weather. The listing says the powder-coated steel resists rust, wind and weather and supports up to 15 pounds per hook.

Three hooks make it the most versatile of the FEED GARDEN poles, and the adjustable range lets you set a lower height for easier refilling. The tradeoff is the same five prongs on a tall pole, and the 15 pound per-hook limit is lower than the Gtongoko 7-prong at 32 pounds at 60 inches. Three loaded hooks also pull the top of the pole to one side.

The pole assembles by sections without tools. Balance the hooks so a heavy feeder on one side is offset on the other, and check the base after storms. Compared with the double-hook FEED GARDEN it adds a hook, and next to the eWonLife it has a wider baffle but only five prongs against nine.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a station with several items on one pole.
cons: Five prongs on a tall pole

products.name: Gtongoko 92 Inch Double Hook Pole 19 Inch Baffle 5-Prong
products.description:
The Gtongoko is unusually clear about limits. It can be assembled at 60, 76 or 92 inches, which leaves about 49.8, 65.8 or 81.8 inches above ground once the 10.2 inch prongs are inserted. Single-hook loads are listed at up to 19 pounds at 60 inches, 18 at 76 and 17 at 92, on a 3/4 inch powder-coated steel pole with a 0.8 mm wall.

A 19 inch baffle and a 16 inch wide double hook sit on a 9.7 inch wide five-prong base. Knowing the load limit stops you from overloading the pole with a heavy hopper. The tradeoff is the thinner 3/4 inch pole compared with the 1 inch poles on the eWonLife and Phikrou, and the lowest hook load of the two Gtongokos.

The maker advises placing the baffle 4 to 5 feet above the ground and the pole 8 to 10 feet from trees, fences and roofs. Distribute weight evenly if both hooks are used. Compared with the 7-prong Gtongoko it carries 13 pounds less at 60 inches, and next to the FEED GARDEN double hook it states a real load.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want published load limits and flexible height.

products.name: Gtongoko 92 Inch Pole 19 Inch Baffle 7-Prong Base

specList.label: Hook load
specList.value: 32 lb at 60, 22 lb at 76, 18 lb at 92

products.description:
This Gtongoko uses a seven-prong base with 9.8 inch prongs and lists higher loads than its five-prong sibling: up to 32 pounds at 60 inches, 22 at 76 and 18 at 92. The 3/4 inch powder-coated steel pole has a 0.8 mm wall and a 19 inch baffle, and the hook is 9.5 inches wide. The assembled heights are 60, 76 or 92 inches, or about 50.2, 66.2 and 82.2 inches above ground.

The 32 pound figure at 60 inches suits large hopper feeders that hold several pounds of seed. The tradeoff is that the load falls to 18 pounds at 92 inches, so the tallest setup is not the strongest. It has a single hook, which limits how much you can hang.

Seven prongs take more effort to install but give a firm hold. Place the baffle 4 to 5 feet above the ground and keep the pole 8 to 10 feet from jump points. Compared with the 5-prong Gtongoko it carries 13 pounds more at 60 inches, and next to the FEED GARDEN triple hook at 15 pounds per hook it is the heavy-duty choice.
products.bestFor: Large hopper feeders hung low on a firm base.
cons: Load falls to 18 pounds at 92 inches

products.name: Phikrou 76 Inch Pole Kit With Squirrel Baffle
products.description:
The Phikrou is a 76 inch kit built from thick 1 inch galvanized steel, which the listing says provides strength and wind resistance. A built-in squirrel baffle is included, and the mounting kit works for classic feeders, smart bird feeders and bluebird houses. The finish is black powder coat that resists rust, rain and UV fading.

The 1 inch pole is thicker than the 3/4 inch Gtongoko poles, so it flexes less under a camera feeder in wind. A ground stake and the hardware are included and the listing says no digging is required. The tradeoff is the shorter 76 inch height and no stated baffle diameter or prong count, which you should check on the product page.

Setup is a stake, sections and a mount, and a heavy camera feeder is the use case it fits best. Check the screws after a season of wind. Compared with the eWonLife at 92 inches it is 16 inches shorter and has fewer hooks, and next to the Gtongoko 7-prong it offers a thicker pole but no published load limit.
products.bestFor: Camera feeders and birdhouses that need a thick, steady pole.
pros: Works with smart feeders and houses

buyingCriteria.explanation: A wide baffle blocks climbers, and wildlife guidance suggests cone baffles at least 17 inches wide. The FEED GARDEN and Gtongoko poles use 19 inch baffles, while the eWonLife uses 16.5 inches with a spring that sinks and wobbles. A baffle should sit about 4 to 5 feet above the ground. Choose 19 inches if squirrels are determined, and the spring if you want added motion defense.

Prongs set grip in soft soil and wind. The eWonLife has nine, the Gtongoko 7-prong has seven, and the FEED GARDEN and Gtongoko 5-prong have five. Prong length also matters, with the Gtongoko prongs 9.8 to 10.2 inches deep. Check the ground where you plant it, and push the base in fully.

Taller poles carry less because of leverage. The Gtongoko 5-prong lists 19 pounds at 60 inches and 17 at 92, and the 7-prong version lists 32 at 60 and 18 at 92. The FEED GARDEN triple hook lists 15 pounds per hook. Pick the lowest height that still keeps the feeder about 5 feet high.

Hooks decide how many items you hang, but each one adds weight at the top. The eWonLife has four sliding hooks, the FEED GARDEN triple has three, the FEED GARDEN double and Gtongoko 5-prong have two, and the Gtongoko 7-prong has one. Balance heavy feeders across hooks. A loaded top bends a thin pole in wind.

Thicker poles resist bending under a camera feeder. The eWonLife and Phikrou use 1 inch tubes, while the Gtongoko uses 3/4 inch with a 0.8 mm wall. Galvanized steel on the Phikrou and powder coat on the others protect against rust. Check for chips and touch up bare spots every season.

A pole only works if squirrels cannot jump around it. Keep it at least 10 feet from trees, shrubs or structures, as the Gtongoko listing says 8 to 10 feet. A baffle does nothing if a shed or fence is close. Also keep the feeder within about 3 feet of a window or more than 30 feet away to reduce collisions.

howWeEvaluated.title: Squirrel defense
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared baffle diameters and types. The FEED GARDEN and Gtongoko models use 19 inch baffles and the eWonLife adds a spring at 16.5 inches. Wildlife guidance suggests at least 17 inches, so the eWonLife earned credit for motion rather than width.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability
howWeEvaluated.description: Prong counts and depth were checked. The eWonLife leads with nine prongs, the Gtongoko 7-prong has seven at 9.8 inches deep, and the others have five. Taller poles with fewer prongs scored lower in soft soil.

howWeEvaluated.title: Load information
howWeEvaluated.description: We used stated hook loads. The Gtongoko models publish loads by height, up to 32 pounds at 60 inches on the 7-prong and 19 pounds on the 5-prong. The FEED GARDEN triple states 15 pounds per hook.

howWeEvaluated.title: Versatility
howWeEvaluated.description: Hook count and adjustability were weighed. The eWonLife has four hooks and a top platform, the FEED GARDEN triple has three hooks and adjusts from 44 to 92 inches, and the Phikrou fits smart feeders and houses.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: Pole thickness and finish were noted. The Phikrou and eWonLife use 1 inch poles and the Gtongoko 3/4 inch. The eWonLife leads on stability, the Gtongoko 7-prong on load, the FEED GARDEN pair on baffle width and value, and the Phikrou on pole thickness.

faq.q: How high should the feeder be?
faq.a: About 5 feet off the ground is common guidance, with a cone baffle below at least 17 inches wide. Keep the pole at least 10 feet from trees or structures squirrels can jump from. Adjustable poles like the FEED GARDEN at 44 to 92 inches or the Gtongoko at 60, 76 or 92 inches let you set the height. A lower setting is easier to refill.

faq.q: Does a baffle really stop squirrels?
faq.a: It stops climbers, but not jumpers. If a shed, fence or branch is within jumping range, the baffle fails. Placement matters as much as baffle width, and the baffle should sit about 4 to 5 feet up. A wide 19 inch cone is harder to bypass than a narrow one.

faq.q: How many prongs do I need?
faq.a: More prongs grip better in soft soil and wind. The eWonLife has nine and the Gtongoko 7-prong has seven, while five is typical. Soil conditions matter more than the count alone, so push the base in fully on firm, level ground. Tamp loose soil around the prongs.

faq.q: What is the load limit on the hook?
faq.a: Check the listing, because it varies. The Gtongoko 7-prong lists up to 32 pounds at 60 inches and 18 at 92, and the FEED GARDEN triple lists 15 pounds per hook. Taller poles carry less. Weigh your feeder when full of seed.

faq.q: Can I hang a camera feeder on these poles?
faq.a: Yes if the pole is sturdy and the weight is within the hook limit. The Phikrou uses a 1 inch galvanized pole and the eWonLife has a wide top platform for smart feeders. A camera feeder adds weight at the top, so use a thicker pole. Check the mount fits before buying.

faq.q: How do I install a pole?
faq.a: Push the base into the ground, screw sections together and slide on the baffle. Some poles say you can step on the prongs to seat them. Loose soil may need extra tamping. Check the pole is vertical after the first rain.

faq.q: How often should I clean what hangs on the pole?
faq.a: Seed feeders should be cleaned about every two weeks, more often in wet weather or if you see sick birds. Use one part bleach to nine parts water, soak about ten minutes, scrub, rinse and dry fully. Wipe the baffle at the same time. Sweep up spilled hulls monthly.
